news.title: Why South Carolina is the wrong starting point for Democrats in 2028
news.text:
The Democratic National Committee is about to make a major blunder regarding the 2028 election by voting soon to formally designate South Carolina as the site of the party’s first presidential primary.

The deliberation last week by the DNC’s Rules and Bylaws Committee yielded 26 votes for South Carolina, 19 for Nevada and four for New Hampshire. Iowa, whose caucuses had long provided the first presidential test, lost its coveted spot after state Democrats botched the vote counting process in 2020. But cementing South Carolina’s status as first in the nation, a shift from its longtime role as first in the South, risks locking Democrats into the wrong focus. 

Diversity is among the Democratic Party’s greatest strengths, but it’s not what early primaries are about. 

While wrangling now over the 2028 calendar might seem premature, exploratory grass-roots campaigning by potential contenders will begin in about six months. Sending them to the right proving ground is pivotal to selecting the most viable Democratic candidate. 

The central argument in South Carolina’s favor is that it is home to many Black voters, a critical bloc for decades in a winning Democratic coalition. The Palmetto State’s share of Black residents, at just over 25%, is roughly double the U.S. average.

In choosing South Carolina, which would hold its primary on Jan. 22, 2028, followed on Feb. 1 by Nevada (where some 31% of the population is Hispanic), the Democratic committee is focusing on the nature of the electorate. The value of the first primary, however, is less about finding out what voters think than it is about learning how candidates perform. 

It’s worth remembering what happened in 2020. Joe Biden flopped in Iowa and New Hampshire, but his campaign was resuscitated when Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn endorsed him in South Carolina, helping Biden win that state’s primary and ultimately his party’s nomination. 

Four years later, a grateful Biden, then president, persuaded the DNC to move South Carolina up to first on its 2024 primary calendar. Biden won there handily and went on to clinch his party’s nomination again before the unraveling that eventually had former Vice President Kamala Harris replace him on the ticket without the benefit of being tested in primaries. 

The ideal lead-off state must have a small population, distributed across easily reachable communities. Local media opportunities need to be focused and affordable. It also helps to have a citizenry that values retail politics. In sum, a state like Iowa. 

I spent considerable time in 2019 and 2020 traipsing around Iowa, covering the Democratic presidential candidates for USA Today and The Wall Street Journal. What I observed was an old-fashioned approach in which candidates were compelled to visit all 99 counties — a rite of passage known as a “Full Grassley,” in honor of Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley, who pioneered the practice. Many Iowans I encountered would not commit unless they had shaken the candidate’s hand — at least twice. 

That sounds quaint, but it’s remarkably revealing. It’s a political version of the NFL combine, where prospective pro football players are tested on skills such as speed and agility long before they get on an actual playing field.

Much is made of the fact that Iowa’s population is roughly 85% white and less progressive than larger coastal states. Yet, Iowa Democrats picked the party’s eventual nominee in all but one presidential contest over the past quarter-century: Al Gore, John Kerry, Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton. (Their record is stronger than that of their Republican counterparts.) The only Democratic “miss” came in 2020, when Iowans chose a brilliant openly gay man, Pete Buttigieg, while rejecting the safe choice in Biden. 

New Hampshire has many of the same virtues for early primaries as Iowa, but its overlap with the Boston media market diminishes its appeal for advertising. 

In announcing plans for 2028, Democratic officials Minyon Moore and James Roosevelt Jr. boasted that they had come up with “the most diverse calendar Democrats have ever had for an open nominating contest.” Diversity is among the Democratic Party’s greatest strengths, but it’s not what early primaries are about. 

It’s a grueling process. But it’s historically one of the best methods of identifying the strongest candidates — or at least weeding out the ones who can’t handle the challenge. 

Once Donald Trump soundly defeated Harris to win a second term, Democrats started counting the days to 2028. Nothing will matter — not diversity or, say, socialism — if the White House can’t be retaken. 

South Carolina’s presentation to the DNC rules committee emphasized Black representation, voting-rights symbolism and the importance of the party’s most loyal constituency. Iowa’s pitch focused on retail politics, affordability and organizational testing. 

The full DNC is scheduled to take up the matter on Aug. 13. It will have to decide if the six “early window” states, with primaries before Super Tuesday, will match last week’s recommendation: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia, in that order. 

For decades most aspiring presidential candidates, especially those with modest name recognition nationally, have focused on the first state, with some effort in the second state. It’s a grueling process. But it’s historically one of the best methods of identifying the strongest candidates — or at least weeding out the ones who can’t handle the challenge. 

The thing about Iowa, which the DNC would be wise to return to the early window, is that it mirrors what Frank Sinatra crooned about New York: If you can make it there, you can make it anywhere.

news.title: Trump administration admits grants for clean energy were canceled based on politics
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration has acknowledged in court documents that it canceled $7.6 billion in grants for hundreds of clean energy projects “based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state” — in this case, 16 states that voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. The canceled projects include $464 million to connect power sources in Minnesota and other states and $50 million to upgrade a North Dakota-Minnesota electrical transmission line.

The statement contradicts repeated assertions by Energy Secretary Chris Wright and other officials that the projects were canceled because they did not adequately advance the nation’s energy needs or had other problems that made them a poor investment of taxpayer dollars.

Democrats and environmental groups seized on the court filing Friday, saying the administration had “weaponized” the federal government to kill good jobs and punish working families because of their political views.

Democrats say what was ‘obvious’ has now been acknowledged

“This administration has now admitted in court what has long been obvious: it terminated nearly 300 cost-cutting energy projects for no reason other than the fact that the states they were in did not vote for the president in the 2024 election,” said Rep. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio and Sen. Patty Murray of Washington state. Both are high-ranking Democrats on the House and Senate Appropriations committees, respectively.

“Weaponizing the federal government like this is outright un-American, and it’s hardworking families already struggling with sky-high costs who are suffering the consequences of this corrupt abuse of power,” Kaptur and Murray said.

They called on congressional Republicans to join them in holding the Trump administration “accountable for the President’s failure to look out for all Americans.”

Related: Green Zone grant awardees announced

The Energy Department announced last October that 321 funding awards across 223 projects were terminated, saying that after review, they “did not adequately advance the nation’s energy needs or were not economically viable.”

The cuts, part of broader attacks from President Donald Trump on climate programs and clean energy funding, slashed federal support for projects to build battery plants, develop hydrogen technology, upgrade the electric grid and capture carbon dioxide emissions.

Russell Vought, the White House budget director, highlighted the cutbacks in a social media post, saying money “to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being cancelled.”

The Energy Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Projects from many states were cut

Projects that were cut were located in California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont and Washington state. All 16 targeted states supported Harris, but Wright said the cuts were “business decisions” based on whether the projects were a good use of taxpayer money or not.

The cuts were immediately challenged in court, and more than two dozen Democratic members of Congress, led by California Sens. Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla and Rep. Zoe Lofgren, wrote a letter to the Energy Department’s acting inspector general requesting a formal investigation. The department’s internal watchdog launched an investigation in December.

Government lawyers had previously confirmed in a court filing late last year that the selection of grants in fact “was influenced by whether a grantee’s address was located in a State that tends to elect … Democratic candidates in state and national elections (so-called “Blue States”).”

Related: Growing pains for clean energy today, payoff tomorrow?

That filing came in a separate suit filed by clean energy groups and the city of St. Paul, Minnesota, over the canceled funding. The most recent admission came in a case called Thakur v. Trump that’s been ongoing since last spring. Federal lawyers acknowledged that they used keywords related to diversity, gender, vaccine hesitancy and COVID-19 to screen for projects that ran afoul of the Trump administration’s priorities.

Holly Bender, chief program officer for the Sierra Club, said the latest court filing shows “the Trump administration is brazenly admitting to a vindictive approach to cancelling much-needed energy infrastructure that ignores the job losses, air pollution and increasing bills that people are experiencing everywhere.”

Instead of “building the energy projects we desperately need,” billions of American taxpayer dollars are “going to line the pockets of a small handful of fossil fuel company CEOs,” Bender said, citing nearly $3 billion pledged by the Trump administration to cancel offshore wind projects in favor of fossil fuel projects such as natural gas and coal.
news.summary:
Trump administration acknowledges it terminated $7.6 billion in grants for clean energy over the political identity of the grant recipient

news.title: States may defy DNC primary calendar as 'nobody is scared' of Ken Martin, CNN reporter says
news.text: CNN's Edward Isaac-Dovere suggested Sunday that states could buck the DNC's primary schedule and hold its elections whenever they want to, pointing to New Hampshire specifically, and said that "nobody" is scared of DNC Chair Ken Martin. "There is the possibility that a state could choose to not follow the DNC here and hold its primary when they want to," Dovere said, as CNN host Manu Raju added that New Hampshire wanted to do this. "And people saying, 'Hey, the DNC is broke. They can't do anything to help us anyway. Nobody is scared in any way of Ken Martin as the chair. And so maybe they'll just go and violate it.' It is not where the infrastructure of the party needs to be for going into 2026 and then 2028," Dovere added. The DNC Rules and Bylaws Committee (RBC) panel, meeting in the nation's capital on Friday, picked South Carolina over Nevada to hold the party's first presidential nominating contest in 2028, a move that will likely maintain a key role in the primary calendar for Black voters, who are a crucial part of the Democrats' base. KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY The decision came after intense lobbying by both states, and by New Hampshire and Iowa over the past year to hold the much-coveted lead-off Democratic primary in the race for the White House. The battle between South Carolina and Nevada was seen as a struggle between rewarding Black voters and outreach to Latino voters, with whom President Donald Trump and Republicans made major gains in the 2024 election, handing Democrats major setbacks. The New Hampshire Democratic Party pointed Fox News Digital to a statement they put out on Friday, in which New Hampshire Democratic Party chair Ray Buckley said that the national party didn't learn anything from 2024. "Today’s vote shows that many party insiders have learned nothing from 2024. New Hampshire has a proven track record of testing our candidates with a rigorous, fair, and efficient process, yet those qualities did not prevail. This committee’s vote does not change the realities governing New Hampshire’s primary, which are beyond the control of both this committee and our state party," Buckley said. Buckley continued, "Democrats’ guiding North Star should be winning general elections, and New Hampshire Democrats will get back to work focusing on the 2026 elections and addressing the significant challenges facing America’s overwhelmed working class. Today’s vote moves the party further away from that objective." SLOTKIN SAYS DEMOCRATIC PARTY NEEDS 'NEW LEADERSHIP': 'OLD MODELS ARE NO LONGER WORKING' Raju asked if Martin would "survive" as chairman. Dovere said that the DNC chair could only be kicked out of the position if he resigned. "He cannot be kicked out, and so it's up to him," he added. The DNC pointed Fox News Digital to a press release from June that highlighted the RBC's vote to strengthen penalties for states and candidates that buck the calendar. The DNC voted at the end of June to strengthen penalties for states who participate in an unsanctioned contest in the early window of the presidential nominating calendar, according to a press release from late June. The rules include implementing a $270,000 fine for any state that hosts an unsanctioned contest and increasing the delegates lost for states that host an unsanctioned contest from 50% to 100%, including all automatic delegates, among others. The penalties also prohibit any candidate participation in DNC debates if they violate the early window rules. DNC CHAIR KEN MARTIN THREW PHONE AT AIDE'S DESK, FACED HR COMPLAINT IN SIGN OF 'FRAYING NERVES': REPORT Martin, while speaking to reporters on Friday, was asked how the DNC would respond, should states such as New Hampshire go rogue. "We have put in significant penalties and sanctions, probably the most enforcement mechanisms ever, to make sure that, you know, folks know we are serious about making sure the calendar we put forth is abided by. Not just by the parties themselves – the state parties – but by also by the candidates," Martin told reporters. He added, "If there’s a consequence to the candidates, right, the candidates are going to have to decide whether or not they want to lose all their delegates in the first four states. Whether they want to lose access to the debate stage. I can’t imagine if one of those states moves into the early window and is not sanctioned, that presidential candidates are going to risk it, risk going there." New Hampshire state law requires that the state hold its primary election at least 7 days before any other state holds a "similar" election. When South Carolina was selected as the first primary state in 2024, New Hampshire defied the DNC and former President Joe Biden left his name off the ballot, though he still won the state as a write-in. While the DNC threatened to withhold New Hampshire's delegates in an effort to get the state to comply, they were ultimately restored in April 2024, ending the feud between the DNC and New Hampshire's Democratic Party in the previous presidential election cycle, according to the AP. Martin faced a formal human resources complaint after allegedly throwing his phone at a junior aide's desk at the party's Washington headquarters in early July, The New York Times reported Sunday. The Times cited six people familiar with the incident, none of whom witnessed it firsthand. Their accounts differed over how forcefully Martin threw the phone, but the newspaper reported that it landed on the aide's desk while Martin was reprimanding the staffer and led to a formal HR complaint. NOTUS also reported on DNC turmoil on Sunday, noting a source briefed on the episode described it as worsening conduct. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's just f---ing unacceptable. This is spiraling behavior," the source told NOTUS. The RNC blasted the national Democratic Party operation in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The DNC is broke, leaderless, and imploding before America’s eyes. From states defying the national party to Ken Martin throwing his phone at staffers, it is undeniable that the inmates are running the asylum. While the Democrat Party collapses, Republicans are united, on offense, and focused on electing our candidates up and down the ballot this November," RNC National Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement.
news.summary: CNN's Edward Isaac-Dovere said states like New Hampshire could defy the DNC primary calendar because "nobody" is scared of Ken Martin as chair.

news.title: Map Shows Democrats' Chances in Key Senate Races With 98 Days to Midterms
news.text: Democrats are facing an uphill battle to take back control of the Senate in the 2026 midterms, as polls show competitive races for Republican-held seats in states like Alaska, Maine, North Carolina and Texas with less than 100 days to go. Historically, the midterms are viewed as a referendum on the sitting president, and President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen amid economic concerns tied to the cost of living and inflation. This has given Democrats hope about their chances of expanding the Senate battleground to flip more conservative states to win a majority in the midterm elections. Bernadette Breslin, press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told Newsweek, “Democrats like Troy Jackson and Josh Turek are the new faces of the Left’s socialist takeover, campaigning on an agenda to raise taxes, green-light reckless spending, and make life even less affordable for American families.” Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, wrote in a statement that Democrats are “well-positioned” in the Senate. “Across the map, we have strong Democratic candidates running formidable campaigns laser-focused on the issues that matter most to voters, from the affordability crisis that Republicans created to the health care access cliff Republicans built when they passed their billionaire tax giveaway bill one year ago,” she said. Democrats Face Difficult Senate Map Despite Favorable Polls Currently, Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate and are eyeing four Democratic-held seats: those in Trump-won Georgia and Michigan, as well as Minnesota and New Hampshire, states he narrowly lost. Democrats view GOP-held seats in Maine, which Trump lost by about 7 points, and North Carolina, which he won by about 3 points, as top targets. No other GOP-held seats are up for grabs in states he either won by single digits or lost in 2024. Even if Democrats hold all of their current seats and flip those two, they would still be held to a 51-49 minority, so they must win in double-digit Trump states to win a majority. Because of that structural hurdle, Republicans have been viewed as the favorites to retain control of the Senate—but that is not seen as a certainty, as several recent polls have given Democrats a wide lead on the generic ballot. The latest poll from Emerson College, for instance, gave Democrats an 11-point lead; a Fox News poll gave Democrats an 8-point lead. Democrats are hoping for such a lead in November that would put states like Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas in play. As of Monday, prediction markets favored Republicans; they had a 55 percent chance of holding onto Senate control on Kalshi and a 56 percent chance on Polymarket. Their chances on Kalshi have narrowed over the past month; on June 27, Republicans had a 58 percent chance of retaining a Senate majority. The following map displays what Kalshi shows for each Senate race that the Cook Political Report views as a toss-up or in its Lean or Likely categories. Of those states, Democrats are best-positioned in Georgia and North Carolina, while Republicans have their best likelihood in Nebraska, where an independent candidate is running. Alaska Alaska voted for Trump in 2024 by 14 points and has not voted Democratic on the presidential level since 1964, so it’s been a reliably Republican state for decades. However, the candidacy of former Representative Mary Peltola, the only Democrat who has won statewide in recent years, has given the party hope about their chances of flipping the state. Alaska has also given Republicans more narrow margins in recent cycles; Trump won it by 10 points in 2020 and 15 points in 2016. Democrats lost the state by 14 points in 2012, 22 points in 2008, 26 points in 2004 and 31 points in 2000. The latest poll from The New York Times and Siena College showed Republican Senator Dan Sullivan leading Peltola by 2 points, 47 percent to 45 percent, with 2 percent backing another candidate and 5 percent unsure. It surveyed 593 likely voters from June 15-29, 2026. An Alaska Survey Research poll, however, showed Peltola with 49.4 percent to Sullivan’s 44.2 percent. It surveyed 1,393 likely voters from June 4-7, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. It is rated a toss-up by Cook. Georgia In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is set to face Representative Mike Collins in the nation’s newest swing state in November. Collins won the GOP primary, but polls give Ossoff an advantage heading into the general election. Trump’s 2-point victory in the key swing state gives Republicans belief that it could be a potential target, but Democrats believe Ossoff’s popularity and Trump’s low approval rating should keep the seat in their hands. The latest surveys show Ossoff, also viewed as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, with a lead as the Cook Political Report has shifted the race to Lean Democrat. An AARP poll found Ossoff leading Collins by 9 points, 52 percent to 43 percent. The poll was conducted on behalf of AARP by Fabrizio Ward, a Republican pollster, and Impact Research, a Democratic pollster. It surveyed 1,060 likely voters across Georgia from July 13-16, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A recent Wick survey showed Ossoff up 4 points, 46.7 percent to 42.9 percent. It surveyed 1,175 likely voters from June 27 to June 30, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. A poll for Fox News put Ossoff's support at 56 percent compared to Collins’ 43 percent—a 13-point margin in the competitive race. It was conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research among 1,002 registered voters from June 23 to 27. Trump carried Georgia by about 2.2 points in the 2024 presidential election, after Democrat Joe Biden won the state by roughly 0.2 points in 2020. Trump won Georgia by about 5 points in 2016, while Republican former Senator Mitt Romney won it by roughly 8 points in 2012 and late Republican Senator John McCain by about 5 points in 2008. Iowa In Iowa, a state Trump won by about 13 points, Republican Representative Ashley Hinson is running against Democratic state Representative Josh Turek to succeed Republican Senator Joni Ernst, who is retiring at the end of her term. Once a battleground, Iowa has shifted toward Republicans, but Democrats believe economic fallout of the Iran war and tariffs could make the state competitive. The latest poll from the Times showed Hinson up 2 points, 48 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 600 likely voters from June 15-27. Meanwhile, a Fox News poll showed Turek up 4 points, 50 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 1,003 registered voters from June 23-27. The Cook Political Report views the race as Lean Republican. Maine Democrats in Maine over the weekend formally selected former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson as their Senate nominee after Graham Platner withdrew from the race after an allegation of sexual assault, which he denied to Newsweek. Jackson’s candidacy offers a potential reset for Democrats, who were deeply concerned about their chances in what they think should be a top pickup opportunity if Platner had stayed in the race. He is running against Republican Senator Susan Collins, viewed as a formidable candidate who has won by wide margins in the past despite the state’s Democratic lean. She has benefited from personal popularity and a moderate image, but Democrats are hoping to tie her to Trump to sink her chances. Republicans have sought to tie Jackson to Platner, as the new nominee supported him in the primary prior to the assault allegations. Only one independent poll has been made public since the candidate switch. A University of New Hampshire poll showed Jackson up 3 points, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 1,178 likely voters from July 15-20. The Cook Political Report classifies the race as a toss-up. Michigan The contours of the Michigan race aren’t quite defined, as the primary is set for August. Trump won Michigan by less than 2 percentage points, so both parties view the state as competitive regardless of the national environment. On the Republican side, former Representative Mike Rogers is viewed as the likely candidate for the general election. Democrats are set to choose between Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate, and public health official Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, in the August primary, which has grown increasingly contentious in recent weeks. The latest poll from Quantus Insights pointed to a close race. Stevens led Rogers by only 1.4 points, 45.1 percent to 43.7 percent, while El-Sayed led Rogers by 1.1 points, 45.2 percent to 44.1 percent. It surveyed 947 Michigan voters from June 29-30, 2026. It’s rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report. Minnesota Democrats are expected to have an advantage in the Minnesota Senate race as Democratic Senator Tina Smith retires. Trump lost Minnesota by about 4 points in 2024, and last voted Republican in 1972. In the Democratic primary, Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan and Representative Angie Craig are facing off in a contested race. Several Republicans are running, but retired sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya has led primary polling. For the general election, a poll from The Minnesota Star-Tribune, KARE-11 and University of Minnesota Hubbard School of Journalism found that 49 percent of Minnesotans would vote for a Democratic candidate for Senate, compared to 41 percent who said they would vote for a Republican. It surveyed 800 likely voters between June 8-10, 2026. The Cook Political Report views the race as Likely Democratic. Nebraska Nebraska GOP Senator Pete Ricketts is facing a challenge from independent Dan Osborn. Osborn lost to GOP Senator Deb Fischer by less than seven points, despite Trump carrying the state by 20 points and the state’s status as reliably Republican. A Tavern Research poll found Osborn leading Ricketts in a two-way race by 5 points, 47 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 1,165 likely voters from May 8-11, 2026. Democrat Cindy Burbank won her party’s primary but will not appear on the ballot in November, opening up a two-way race. Although Osborn does not have ties to either party, he is viewed as less conservative than Ricketts and has received support from Democrats in the state. Burbank’s withdrawal from the race could prevent a split among anti-Ricketts voters. The Cook Political Report views the race as Likely Republican. New Hampshire New Hampshire backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by nearly 3 points in 2024, but the retirement of longtime Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat, has left an open race that Republicans see as a possible flip opportunity. Democratic Representative Chris Pappas is viewed as the Democratic front-runner, while former Senators John Sununu and Scott Brown are running in the Republican primary. The latest Saint Anselm College poll gave Pappas a lead against each candidate. He led Brown by 12 points, 48 percent to 36 percent and Sununu by 6 points, 47 percent to 41 percent. It was conducted from June 24-25, 2026, among 1,614 registered voters across the state. A University of New Hampshire poll showed Pappas up 14 points over Brown, 52 percent to 38 percent and 3 points over Sununu, 47 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 2,232 likely voters from June 18-23. The Cook Political Report classifies the race as Lean Democrat. North Carolina Democrats haven’t won a Senate race in North Carolina since 2008, but former Governor Roy Cooper’s candidacy as a popular, statewide-elected official has fueled party optimism about their chances of winning in November against incumbent Republican Thom Tillis. The race is now viewed as Lean Democrat by the Cook Political Report. The latest poll from the Times showed Cooper up 7 points, 50 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 601 likely voters from June 15-27. A Public Policy Polling survey, conducted among 759 voters from July 10-11, showed Cooper leading by 4 points, 48 percent to 44 percent. Ohio In Ohio, former Senator Sherrod Brown is seeking a comeback after losing in 2024. He is challenging Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to replace Vice President JD Vance. Ohio was once a major battleground but has shifted rightward over the past decade, backing Trump by about 11 points in 2024. The Times found Husted with a 3-point lead, 50 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 601 likely voters from June 15-28, 2026. An AARP poll showed Brown up 3 points, 48 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 800 registered voters from June 14-16, 2026. The Cook Political Report rates Ohio as a toss-up. Texas Texas backed Trump by 14 points last year, but Democrats believe state Representative James Talarico will be competitive against Republican nominee Paxton, the state attorney general who has faced some scandals and an impeachment in the state’s GOP-led legislature. The Lone Star State has for decades been viewed as solidly conservative, but it has shifted toward becoming less so due to growth in cities like Austin, Dallas and Houston, as well as their suburbs becoming more competitive. However, rightward shifts among the state’s Latino population boosted Trump’s performance in the state in 2024. A poll from the Times showed a tight race with each candidate receiving 47 percent support. It surveyed 656 likely voters from June 19-27, 2026. A Texas Politics Project poll found Paxton up by a single point, 43 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 1,200 registered voters from June 5-12, 2026. The race is viewed as Lean Republican by the Cook Political Report. Why Democrats Believe They Can Flip the Senate Trump’s approval rating is a major reason Democrats believe they can compete for control of the Senate in this year’s midterms. His popularity has declined since he returned to office in January 2025 due to economic concerns, including tariffs, the cost of living and higher gas prices amid the war in Iran. Trump campaigned on bringing prices down as the country grappled with a high inflation rate in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, and his focus on cost-of-living issues helped carry him to victory in key swing states. But as the midterms approach, polling shows most Americans remain unhappy with the state of the economy and Trump’s presidency overall. A new poll from YouGov and CBS News found that 61 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump, while 39 percent approve of him. Among independents, 27 percent approved of Trump compared to 73 percent who disapproved of him in the poll. When it came to the economy specifically, 35 percent of respondents said they approved of Trump compared to 65 percent who disapproved of him. It surveyed 2,193 adults from July 22-24, 2026. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Polls point to close races for Republican-held seats in states like Maine, North Carolina and Texas ahead of the midterms.

news.title: How the Big Beautiful Bill became law: Trump locks horns with GOP lawmakers
news.text:
Indeed, Trump ratcheted up the pressure. In late May, the president addressed the Republican House conference, in which he lambasted the SALT deduction and told the group of Republican holdouts to fall in line.

Yet Trump’s badgering, which even featured him telling Lawler that he knew his Hudson Valley district better than the congressman did, backfired.

LaLota told the Washington Examiner that Trump had a prepared speech to deliver to the conference, but threw it aside and launched into his own 45-minute speech, about half of which was a diatribe against the SALT deduction.

LaLota said Trump used the moment to raise the temperature on those five “saltiest” holdouts in the SALT caucus. LaLota recalled that, after the 45-minute haranguing, he was “a bit anxious that maybe our coalition might be fractured a little bit.”

But instead, the pressure campaign made the group “circle the wagons,” Garbarino told the Washington Examiner.

The group huddled in the back of the conference room after Trump spoke. There, Kim dug her heels in and rallied the others to join her in terms that belied her reputation as a soft-spoken lawmaker. 

“She pointed at all of us and says, ‘Nobody talks to us like that,’ and ‘We’re not folding, we’re going to get everything we need out of this,’” LaLota said.

Kim, a South Korea-born lawmaker who represents one of the competitive districts in the country, normally avoids swearing in public, she told the Washington Examiner. But she broke that rule. 

“And I said, ‘Bulls***,’” Kim recalled. “I’m using the four-letter words, and I’m supposed to be a very nice, submissive, quiet Asian-American female, you know, but I just, I guess, shattered all of their thinking.”

“Like, ‘Oh my God! If she’s using four-letter words, this must be really serious,’” Kim said.

LaLota said it was a “rallying cry” for the saltiest five negotiators.

During an interview with the Washington Examiner, Lawler recounted that Trump locked eyes with him during the fateful speech.

“I was sitting kind of fourth row, dead center, looking at the podium that he was speaking from, and a few minutes into the meeting, he, you know, caught my eye and effectively started going down the path of telling me that I just have to accept that SALT wasn’t going to happen in the bill,” Lawler said.

“He kept going on and on and on about SALT and how bad the blue states are, and it’s a tax giveaway to the blue states,” he added.

House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-MN) characterized the Trump-Lawler exchange as “a great back and forth.”

After Trump said he knew Lawler’s district better than he did, the congressman, who is known to take on lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, said that there was a “quite extensive” back-and-forth. At one point, then-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-GA) jumped into the fray and said the president never promised to lift the SALT cap.

“And I corrected her and pointed out that, in fact, he did campaign on lifting the cap on SALT when he was in Nassau County doing a rally,” said Lawler, who represents a district won by Kamala Harris in 2024. “He talked about it.”

Lawler said that as Trump met with the conference and spoke about SALT, he was actively texting House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and Trump’s staff to make it clear that he was not changing his position.

“And in fact, if they proceed forward without changing the text from what the Ways and Means Committee put forth, I would be a no on the bill,” Lawler said.

Garbarino and LaLota told the Washington Examiner that they would also have voted no on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act if it didn’t contain agreeable changes to the SALT cap. 

“Would we have voted against the bill if it didn’t have SALT in it? I would,” Garbarino said. “I know I would have. I mean, if it kept the cap at 10, I would have had to have — I would be packing my desk up already.”

In 2017, a dozen House Republicans from high-tax states such as California and New York voted against the first Trump tax cut bill because it capped the SALT deduction. 

‘You get the football, you run as hard as you can’

Negotiations over the SALT cap were some of the trickiest that Republicans faced in advancing the fiscal overhaul through reconciliation, a legislative process that allows bills to bypass the filibuster and pass with only a simple majority in the Senate.

The majority of House Republicans and all Senate Republicans not only oppose raising the cap on SALT deductions but also favor eliminating the deductions altogether. They argue that allowing filers to deduct state and local taxes from their federal taxable income only subsidizes excess spending on the part of liberal states such as New York and California.

And to raise from $10,000 to $40,000 was a big process.

The SALT agreement is an increase from the amount the Ways and Means Committee approved during markup. That bill agreed to increase the $10,000 SALT cap to $30,000 for married couples and set an income limit of $400,000. While the proposal would have tripled the SALT cap, the five “saltiest” Republicans remained steadfast, maintaining that $30,000 was too low.

Still, the only supporter of raising the SALT cap who was also on the Ways and Means Committee during this process was Rep. Nicole Malliotakis (R-NY). She told the Washington Examiner that $30,000 was a good get given the makeup of the committee, and compared the process to a football or a basketball game.

“One out of 27 wanted SALT,” Malliotakis said of negotiations in Ways and Means.

“You get the football, you run as hard as you can, and then you know somebody else takes it,” she said of her efforts. 

Still, the core five saltiest members wanted more than what Ways and Means had proposed. 

Malliotakis joked that at one point she was almost evicted from the SALT caucus. “I was voted off the island,” she quipped.

Kim said that, for her in particular, the stakes were high, which was why she and the other four “saltiest” members were so dug in on getting an even higher cap.

That is because, similar to New York, California is a high-tax state whose residents would disproportionately benefit from raising the cap, unlike those in states such as Texas. And while New York had representation in the caucus from Lawler, LaLota, and Garbarino, she was the only one from the Golden State.

“I was representing the entire state of California by then,” Kim said.

She said that there was a lot of weight on her shoulders.

“I knew we needed to get this done, even to much of the criticism that I was hearing back home: ‘Why are you holding up the bill? What’s wrong with the whole bill?’ I go, ‘I’m not voting it down; it’s just I’m fighting for you guys,’” Kim said. “This is something I ran on.”

‘Raised voices’ in the negotiations

Garbarino said the negotiations would get quite passionate at times.

“There’s always raised voices when you deal with a bunch of New Yorkers,” he joked. “Definitely people walked out, people, you know, didn’t come back — I mean, you had different people fighting at different points.”

Garbarino said that the only people who kept their calm most of the time during negotiations were the leadership suite — Johnson, Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-LA), and Whip Tom Emmer. 

“I don’t think we yelled at each other, that’s not right, but we definitely got frustrated and passions — I mean, I heard Kim curse once, I mean, Young Kim doesn’t curse, so … people definitely got heated, passionate,” Garbarino said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who was then a GOP senator from Oklahoma, acted as a go-between during negotiations with SALT members and the Senate. Notably, no Republicans on the Senate side were fans of raising the $10,000 SALT cap, but negotiators knew there had to be changes because, without the SALT caucus, they wouldn’t have enough votes in the House to pass the bill.

LaLota described Mullin as “an ambassador of sorts” who had a “high degree of trust” among House members. Before Mullin became a senator in 2023, he spent a decade in the House and had forged relationships with many who are still in the lower chamber.

“He was great to work with,” Garbarino said of Mullin. “I mean, he knew we had to get something done, so he was trying to convince his colleagues that this was something.”

During the meetings and during her interview with the Washington Examiner, Kim wore a pin featuring literal salt. She even had salt packets that she would hand out to remind everyone exactly what her priorities were.

Everyone had ‘a different role to play’

As a deal was closing in, Lawler said the team was at the Treasury Department three times within 24 hours. There was a strategy to the negotiations, and the SALT team was in constant communication.

“Nick, for instance, can be a hard-charging bull at times, and you know played that role appropriately throughout,” Lawler said.

For instance, LaLota said that he skipped the last of the three meetings that led to the deal being inked. He said that was partially a negotiating tactic.

LaLota said that, after the second meeting, he felt the other side was trying to paint the SALT lawmakers into a corner, so he boycotted the next meeting in protest. He said that, with the benefit of hindsight, that “kind of solidified our position.”

“Everybody in the negotiating team had a different role to play,” he said. “I was the bad cop a couple different times.”

Kim said that despite LaLota’s absence, he was still listening in on the meeting on speaker phone.

Lawler said that Kim, who is always “very professional, very courteous,” got “heated” at times during the negotiations.

“And I think, frankly, that was good — it showed that we were not going to buckle and not going to cave,” he said.

The group also had a couple of different group chats to discuss strategy.

“We started with the larger SALT caucus group chat, and then it started getting smaller and smaller,” Kim said, until it was just the “big five.”

Kim said one of the group chats was titled “saltiest” and consisted of her, Lawler, LaLota, Garbarino, and Kean.

LaLota said that the group chats evolved over time.

“Different members throughout the last couple of years had expressed an interest to be supportive, but ultimately the five of us were the ride-or-die group, ultimately, the five of us weren’t going to cave in until we got the $40,000 that we were bargaining for,” LaLota said. “So yes, there was a decent group chat amongst us.” 

A deal is struck

In the end, the deal that was reached raised the SALT cap to $40,000 for five years and included a $500,000 income threshold.

Garbarino said getting the cap to $40,000 was a big deal for his district, even with the five-year sunset.

“I think we’re very happy with what we got, rather than $30,000 forever, because the $40,000 really covers a lot of people, especially my district and other districts,” Garbarino said.

He pointed out that the standard deduction for a married couple is now just over $32,000.

“So, I mean, it would have been less than what the state deduction is,” Garbarino said.

He also said the $500,000 income threshold cap helped dispel arguments that the changes primarily benefited millionaires and billionaires. 

Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith (R-MO) said that several SALT members have told him since passage that his permanent remedy “would have been better” than the final version. “No one knows what’s going to happen in five years.”

Kim made a point of highlighting how Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-NY), a close ally of Trump, got significantly involved near the end and helped the caucus reach a deal.

“She came in, and then of course, in one of our last few meetings, it really helped that she was there,” Kim said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who was heavily involved in the SALT talks, noted that the House had to battle with the Senate, which “had no interest in SALT.

“Those blue-state Republicans did a fantastic job of representing their constituency,” Bessent told the Washington Examiner.

Sen. James Lankford (R-OK) said of the House SALT members, “We all understood their perspective, where they were, and what their constituents are feeling. They’re representing their constituents.”

Garbarino recalled that after the deal was finally reached, he was happy to be done but “mentally exhausted.” Still, a group of those who negotiated the deal went out for drinks at Joe’s Seafood, a high-end hot spot near the White House that is popular with lawmakers, lobbyists, and Washington power brokers.

“A few of us from the SALT states, as well as the White House … we walked out to [Joe’s] and got a martini or a drink,” Garbarino said. “It was mentally exhausting, so we went and had a nice cocktail afterwards — we earned it!”

While Garbarino had a martini, Lawler said he didn’t remember exactly what he ordered, but surmised that it was probably a glass of red wine, if anything.

Kim said she didn’t go out after the win because she doesn’t drink.

“And I’m like, ‘Just don’t do anything I wouldn’t do’ — I’m a mom, I’m a grandma,” Kim joked. “‘You know, I’m watching you even though I’m not there.’ And then I sent them off to celebrate because we thought we got a good deal there.”

Lawler said he saw the president again the day after a deal was reached while in the Cabinet room to discuss other provisions in the bill.

“The president once again kind of caught my eye, and he looked at me, says, ‘You know, Lawler, you did a good job. You cut a good deal. You knew when to say yes, but you made it too big of a deal. All I heard was SALT, SALT, SALT, SALT.’”

“And I looked at him, and I said, ‘Mr. “President, I read The Art of the Deal,” and he paused and said, ‘You did a good job,’” Lawler recalled with a laugh.

news.title: Trump visits Michigan amid feud over Canada tariffs and new border bridge
news.text:
President Donald Trump visits suburban Detroit Monday, aiming to champion his economic record and defend sweeping tariffs. This trip to a pivotal swing state comes as these policies have hurt many local businesses, with midterm election season heating up.

His itinerary includes a stop at a General Motors facility in Milford, home to vehicle testing grounds. Before his speech, he will observe a drag race demonstration, a prelude to an IndyCar race in Washington next month, promoted for America's 250th birthday.

Early voting is underway for Michigan's August 4 primary, featuring fierce nomination contests in both major parties.

Republican Mike Rogers is unopposed in the Senate primary. However, the GOP gubernatorial race pits President Trump-backed Rep. John James against Perry Johnson, a businessman who previously launched unsuccessful campaigns. Johnson attempts to emulate the president's style, despite lacking endorsement, even planning a "Trump Tailgate" outside the GM event.

The Democratic Senate primary, between Rep. Haley Stevens and progressive Abdul El-Sayed, has drawn national attention. The winner will challenge Rogers, who lost narrowly to Democrat Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024.

Trump's new Canada tariffs could hurt Michigan

Michigan was one of the 2024 battlegrounds Trump flipped after it backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. But the state has also seen parts of its economy affected by the president's tariffs, including on imported cars and auto parts.

A new round of steep import levies is taking effect on dozens of U.S. trading partners. But Trump has singled out Canada with tariffs as high as 50% on a wide array of its products, including cars.

The president is visiting Oakland County, which encompasses much of Detroit's northern suburbs. Once a Republican stronghold, it has increasingly leaned Democratic, backing Biden against Trump in 2020 and Vice President Kamala Harris against Trump four years later.

The Milford area home to the GM facility hosting Trump is suburban enough that, in a wooded space nearby, a convincing wooden structure painted all in black and shaped like bigfoot seems to be emerging toward a major road. The White House says Trump will talk up having generated manufacturing jobs and foreign investment in the U.S. while making the case that his policies and leadership have boosted the auto industry.

"The President pledged to put Michigan workers back to work, and he's doing it," White House spokesperson Liz Huston said in a statement.

Michigan's economy relies heavily on Canada, however, meaning the new tariffs — coupled with inflation still running high and gas prices rising again as the already unpopular war in Iran escalates — have created additional economic concerns statewide.

Those come at a time when voters across the country were already increasingly dissatisfied with Trump's handling of the economy.

Jason Roe, a former executive director of the Michigan Republican Party who tried unsuccessfully to distance it from Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement in 2021, said that more than coinciding with his new round of tariffs, Trump's visit is a function of Michigan's relatively late primary and is meant to ensure that James secures the nomination.

But Roe also predicted that it was a risk for the president to tie himself too closely to top Republicans ahead of the general election, calling it "kryptonite to November voters."

Trump, who won the White House on a promise to lower the cost of living, also has seen his approval ratings sag, meaning kitchen table issues could be a liability for Republicans trying to hold control of Congress after Election Day on Nov. 3.

"We're happy to have the president here, campaigning with Republicans. We think it highlights the fact that the only thing they care about is Donald Trump and refuse to stand up to him," said Curtis Hertel, chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party. "It's good for us every time the president is here because he's incredibly unpopular."

The US and Canada have squabbled over a new border bridge

The Supreme Court struck down many of Trump's sweeping tariffs, but his administration has tried to find ways around that, including by arguing that he can impose them on Canada because that country is discriminating against American exports of products including automobiles.

But Trump's latest round of tariffs came after he voiced frustration with Canada for having retaliated and imposed its own levies on U.S. imports in response to Trump's initial tariffs last year. Trump launched the first round after alleging Canada should do more to stop fentanyl smuggling.

It is Trump's third trip to Michigan in his second term.

In January, he visited a Ford plant in Dearborn and addressed the Detroit Economic Club, offering a defense of tariffs even as auto industry leaders blamed them for increasing the cost of doing business. The outcry is part of the reason Trump extended rebates to domestic car companies on some tariffs on imported auto parts.

The president marked his second term's first 100 days with a rally in Warren, where he mostly mentioned grievances left over from the 2024 campaign, even scoffing at what Biden might look like in a bathing suit.

His latest visit coincides with tensions between his administration and Canada that have marred the opening of a new bridge linking Detroit and Windsor, Ontario.

Canada on Friday held its own event hailing the opening of the $4.7 billion Gordie Howe International Bridge instead of a planned celebration with officials in the U.S. after Trump announced the new Canadian tariffs.

An earlier, joint ceremony had been set for June but was scrapped after Trump suggested the U.S. wanted a "better" deal on the bridge it co-owns with Canada.

That eventually led to an agreement on splitting tolls that was supposed to allow for the rescheduled joint U.S.-Canada celebration — until the new tariffs derailed that, too.
news.author: Will Weissert

news.title: Another Abrego Garcia: Man Unlawfully Deported Twice
news.text:
A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.

Now Lost in Salvadoran Prison System

A new court order Friday in federal court in south Texas, first flagged by Politico’s Kyle Cheney, reveals that another Salvadoran national has been unlawfully deported twice by the Trump administration in the past eight months in violation of separate orders by a federal judge and an immigration judge.

In an under-the-radar case reminiscent of the brutalization of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, Nelson Ariel Umanzor Chavez was deported to Mexico in November despite a federal court’s temporary restraining order barring the administration from removing him from the United States. As in the Abrego Garcia case, the court ordered the administration to facilitate his return from Mexico and he was in fact returned to the U.S. by the end of November.

But then in January — despite a 2019 immigration court order barring his removal to his native country because he was “more likely than not to be tortured” there — the administration deported him to El Salvador anyway, where he was immediately imprisoned. 

His condition and the exact location of his detention remain unknown.

“Salvadoran authorities have transferred Petitioner between prisons and his family has not been provided information regarding his current location, his condition, or whether he is alive,” according to the latest court order, citing a declaration filed in the case. 

Umanzor Chavez unlawfully entered the United States in 2015 but was released as an unaccompanied minor. His asylum claim was rejected in 2019, but he was granted withholding of removal to El Salvador under the Convention Against Torture. He appears from the court order to have remained free for a decade, until he was detained in May 2025 in Baltimore during an ICE check-in. 

In his order Friday laying out the circumstances of the case, U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. (a Trump appointee) denied the relief Umanzor Chavez was seeking because his request was based on his earlier deportation to Mexico, not his more recent deportation to El Salvador. The judge gave him until next month to amend his pleadings to challenge the second deportation.

Houston ICE Shooting: No Drugs in Van

The substance that the FBI found in the work van being driven by Lorenzo Salgado Araujo when he was shot and killed by an ICE agent tested negative for narcotics or illicit drugs, the House district attorney announced Friday. The fact that the news came not from the FBI but from the local prosecutor reinforced suspicions that the Trump administration had tried to sully the victim’s reputation. For reasons which remain unclear, the search warrant for the van which revealed the FBI’s suspicion of meth was unsealed unusually early in the case amidst outrage over the shooting.

ICE Plans to Target Haitians

With the Supreme Court ending Temporary Protected Status (TPS) protection for more than 300,000 Haitians, ICE is planning for a potential arrest and deportation blitz, CBS News reports.

Boat Strike Watch: Grisly Stats Edition

A new report from the Washington Office on Latin America says the death toll from President Trump’s lawless high seas campaign against alleged drug-smuggling boats is 221. 

But despite the illegal carnage, the campaign is failing to achieve its own stated objective of strangling drug trafficking by sea, the WaPo reports:

The Trump administration’s deadly military strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats have not reduced the amount of cocaine entering the United States, but they’re prompting criminal organizations to develop new strategies and tactics and undermining traditional investigative methods, according to a previously unreported assessment by the Drug Enforcement Administration, a closed-door congressional briefing and interviews with current and former U.S. and foreign officials.

Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon

NYT: An Admiral’s Rise Reveals the Politics Driving Hegseth’s Pentagon

WaPo: After Trump’s order, West Point curbed faculty speech. One professor said no.

NYT Still Crushing It on Air Force One

Undaunted by the Trump DOJ’s unlawful subpoenaing of five of its reporters, the New York Times continues to crank out new stories on President Trump’s scandalous new Air Force One boondoggle:

Inside the Rushed Effort to Get Trump His New Air Force One

Iranian Threat to Air Force One Prompted Plane Swap During NATO Summit

In Rush to Track Down Leaks, Justice Dept. Reversed Its Own Process

Exporting the MAGA Vision Abroad

Barnes and deputy assistant secretary Samuel Samson — who were being dispatched by the Trump administration “on a mission to cast doubt on the fairness and integrity of the country’s electoral system” ahead of the Oct. 4 presidential election, the WaPo reports.

Trump Loses on Election Meddling Gambit

The 1st Circuit Court of Appeals handed the administration an important loss Friday when it declined to pause a lower court order that blocked the administration from moving ahead on President Trump’s executive order purporting to revamp mail voting ahead of the midterm elections.

news.title: How Red and Blue States Compare on Cost of Living
news.text: With a majority of U.S. voters expressing deep concern over inflation and the rising cost of groceries and gas, according to recent polling, economic affordability is shaping up as a decisive issue for this year's midterm election. Democrats are looking to leverage these frustrations against Republicans, much as the issue fueled political shifts in 2024. In the wake of rising energy prices following the start of the Iran war in late February, Americans are pessimistic about the direction taken by the U.S. economy, with 44 percent saying the economic conditions in the country today are “poor,” according to the latest Gallup survey. A Fox News Poll conducted between July 17-20 found that 54 percent of registered voters surveyed believed Democrats would better handle the economy than Republicans, who were at 45 percent, indicating Americans want change. An even bigger majority (67 percent) in Fox News' poll disapproved of how President Donald Trump is handling the economy, as his approval rating remains near record low. However, data from the Newsweek American Dream Index reveals that the cost of living is notably higher in blue-leaning states while remaining relatively lower in red and battleground states. Understanding the American Dream Index The Newsweek American Dream Index evaluates all 33,772 U.S. ZIP codes on a scale from 0 to 100 across six core pillars of opportunity: For this article, however, we are going to look at the cost of living only—one of the factors considered in the overall scores. How High the Cost of Living Is in Red and Blue States The cost of living measures how far a U.S. household can stretch a paycheck. As a quick rule of thumb to interpret the scores: Among the states with the lowest score for cost of living, where households are struggling or facing challenges, are Hawaii (24.1), California (25.2), New York (27.7), New Jersey (30.7), Florida (31.1), Washington (33.2), and Oregon (34.1). All of these states, with the exception of Florida, voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris, a Democrat, in the 2024 presidential election and have been traditionally considered “blue,” or Democratic-leaning. On the other hand, states with the highest score for cost of living, where households are doing well and thriving, are in states that voted for Trump in 2024 and are generally considered “red” or Republican-leaning, such as North Dakota (74.7), Iowa (74.3), and South Dakota (72.1). But the cost of living is not all that voters will be considering when they head to the ballot in November. States like Hawaii, California, and New York have slightly higher scores for economic mobility (82.1, 68.0, and 68.5, respectively) than North Dakota (75.2), Iowa (64.5), or South Dakota (67.7) and score better on education (with Hawaii, California, and New York at 61.6, 62.6, 65.6, respectively, while North Dakota, Iowa, and South Dakota are at 54.9, 54.7, and 54.4, respectively).
news.summary: The cost of living is shaping up to be a key issue in the November midterms, and one that could backfire against Republicans.

news.title: The Democratic National Committee Is Imploding
news.text:
The Democrat Party has spent months promising a blue wave midterm election and projecting confidence, but behind closed doors, the Democratic National Committee is in turmoil.

According to a New York Times report, the Democratic National Committee can't pay its bills and Chairman Ken Martin is paranoid and unhinged. In other words, the committee is drowning in internal chaos.

This is threatening to blunt whatever momentum Democrats thought they had heading into the midterms, which are now just 100 days away.

PJ Media previously reported that the DNC put up its own DC headquarters as collateral for a $15 million line of credit last year. That was bad news on its own. But it's gotten worse. Party leaders have now asked vendors to hold off sending invoices until after the midterms, according to three people briefed on the discussions.

And then there’s the issues with Chairman Martin. According to the report, he has become isolated, anxious about his job security, and dependent on a shrinking circle of trusted aides. More than two dozen current and former Democrats and DNC officials described his behavior to the New York Times, most speaking anonymously because nobody wants their name near this dumpster fire.

And who could blame them?

Just how unhinged has Martin become? Well, in early July, Martin allegedly threw his phone at a junior aide's desk while reprimanding him, prompting a formal HR complaint. Accounts differ on how hard he threw it, though everyone agrees it hit the desk, not the aide. Martin later met with HR about his behavior. The DNC declined to comment, and Martin declined an interview request.

ICYMI: Tucker Carlson Has Gone Bat Poop Crazy, Wants Trump Tried for Treason

Martin has also made dark jokes about how long he'll last as chairman, even though his term runs through 2029, but he still insists he's committed to the party and hopeful about November.

The big problem for the Democrats, of course, is the money gap with Republicans. President Donald Trump controls a $400 million super PAC. The Republican National Committee reported $128.5 million in cash on hand. The DNC is $2 million in debt. Before filing its July report, the DNC even transferred $1 million out of its 2028 convention fund to prop up its main accounts.

The loan hasn't helped.

The DNC has paid more than $700,000 in interest on that $15 million line of credit, averaging over $75,000 a month, and starting in January it owes $1.66 million in principal payments every month. The DNC has funneled money to its House and Senate campaign arms every cycle for more than a decade, but officials have privately told congressional leaders that won't happen in 2026.

There isn't any cash left to give, and a big factor in this debacle is Kamala Harris. In 2024, Kamala Harris raised a ton of money in her campaign but left behind millions in debt that the DNC spent much of last year paying down with her help. Last fall, Martin sent $3 million each to Democratic gubernatorial campaigns in Virginia and New Jersey, structuring the loan for those transfers, hoping the wins would revive DNC fundraising.

The bet hasn't paid off yet.

Martin's paranoia bled into his own team. This spring, he confronted the party's finance director over what he believed was an effort to push him out. In May, finance chairman Chris Korge was already talking with other officers about an emergency meeting on the party's finances. Martin read those talks as a plot against him, and when the two finally spoke late one Tuesday night, things got ugly fast.

The emergency meeting Korge wanted eventually happened in Pittsburgh in June. For the first time, party officers had to sign nondisclosure agreements just to be in the room. I wrote before that this was the sign of a huge problem. Well, there’s the proof.

Make no mistake about it, the Democratic National Committee is a dumpster fire right now. It’s deep in debt, can't pay its vendors on time, and its chairman is a paranoid wreck who needs nondisclosure agreements to keep its own board members quiet.

We’re 100 days out from the midterms, hardly enough time for things to turn around for the Democratic National Committee. This is gonna be fun to watch.

news.title: The Energy Department Admits the OMB Canceled Grants 'Solely' To Punish Trump's Political Opponents
news.text:
Last September, the Department of Energy (DOE) recommended cancellation of 624 grants for clean energy projects that had been approved by the Biden administration. After reviewing the list, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) winnowed it down to 284 grants, all but one of which had been awarded to projects in states that were represented by Democrats in the U.S. Senate and had voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

"No decisions were made on politics," Energy Secretary Chris Wright improbably insisted during a House hearing on June 10. "I keep hearing that charge. It's bullshit." While that might have been true of the DOE's original list, it was not true of the grant terminations that the OMB ultimately approved. A month after Wright's testimony, DOE Principal Deputy General Counsel Jeff Novak admitted that the OMB's decisions about which grants to cancel were "based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state," as opposed to "any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor."

That admission, which The New York Times highlighted on Friday, was part of the DOE's July 15 stipulations in Thakur v. Trump, a case brought by University of California researchers who are fighting to retain their federal grants. In a June 4 lawsuit, the researchers argued that the Trump administration's "mass termination of grants," which was presented as part of the cost-cutting steps taken by the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency, illegally usurped congressional powers.

To avoid discovery in that case, the Energy Department agreed to a list of stipulations, focusing on the grants that the OMB decided to nix in October. "Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left's climate agenda is being cancelled," OMB Director Russell Vought bragged in an October 1 post on X. Vought listed 16 affected states, all of which had awarded their electoral votes to Harris in 2024.

That was no mere coincidence, Novak confirms. The DOE's "624-grant list included proposals to terminate awards with a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in States that awarded their electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and [had] two Democratic-caucusing Senators," he writes, along with "awards with a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a State that awarded its electoral votes to President Trump in the 2024 election or [had] at least one Republican-caucusing Senator." The OMB list of 284 targets, by contrast, omitted grants in the latter category.

"With one exception," Novak says, "the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and [had] two Democratic-caucusing Senators." Those canceled grants included awards to two of the plaintiffs in Thakur v. Trump. The remaining 340 grants on the DOE's list, all of which involved states that went for Trump in 2024 or had at least one Republican senator, "were not terminated in October 2025, and they have not since been terminated."

That distinction, Novak concedes, "was not based on a rational connection between the recipient's location and/or place of performance and DOE's past or current agency priorities." Nor was it consistent with the approach that the DOE had taken. "The political identity of the grant recipient's state was not a factor that DOE's program offices considered in evaluating whether to retain, modify, or terminate grants," Novak says. "DOE's program offices had proposed to terminate similarly situated Blue State and non-Blue State grants."

Last December in St. Paul v. Wright, another case involving the OMB's cancellation of DOE grants, the government's lawyers similarly conceded that "the selection of which DOE grant termination decisions were included in the October 2025 notice tranche was influenced by whether a grantee's address was located in a State that tends to elect and/or has recently elected Democratic candidates in state and national elections." But they argued that "consideration of partisan politics is constitutionally permissible" because "it can serve as a proxy for legitimate policy considerations."

According to Novak's stipulations, the OMB's list not only was "influenced" by whether grant recipients were located in blue states; it was determined "solely" by that consideration. That admission undermines the already dubious suggestion that the OMB viewed a state's "partisan politics" as "a proxy for legitimate policy considerations," especially since Novak says the OMB's decisions were not based on "any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor."

The plaintiffs in St. Paul v. Wright argued that such politically motivated grant terminations are unconstitutional. "Under bedrock equal protection principles, the government must have some legitimate state interest when it treats one group differently from a similarly situated group," they said. "Bare animus, political or otherwise, is not a legitimate government interest. Animus and political retribution are the only explanations for the differential treatment of terminated and non-terminated DOE awardees here."

That lawsuit also contended that the grant cancellations violated the First Amendment. The plaintiffs cited the Supreme Court's unanimous 2024 ruling in National Rifle Association v. Vullo, which involved a state regulator's attempts to discourage financial institutions from doing business with the NRA. "The First Amendment prohibits government officials from wielding their power selectively to punish or suppress speech," the Court said, whether "directly or (as alleged here) through private intermediaries." In this case, the complaint in St. Paul v. Wright said, "Defendants have targeted private intermediaries—including Plaintiffs—to punish the speech of the citizens of the states where grantees reside or where the DOE awards would be carried out."

In January, Amit P. Mehta, a federal judge in the District of Columbia, ruled that the plaintiffs did not have standing to pursue the First Amendment claim. But he found in their favor on the Fifth Amendment equal protection claim, saying the government's distinction between blue and red states failed even under the highly deferential "rational basis" test that applies in such cases when they do not involve "suspect classes" such as race.

"The parties do not dispute that Defendants drew a classification between grantees located in Blue States and grantees located in Red States," Mehta wrote. "Without more, there is no reason to believe that terminating an award to a recipient located in a state whose citizens tend to vote for Democratic candidates—and, particularly, voted against President Trump—furthers the agency's energy priorities any more than terminating a similar grant of a recipient in a state whose citizens tend to vote for Republican candidates or voted for President Trump. There is no evidence that Plaintiffs, for example, receive more funding than other grantees or use the funding for projects the agency views as uniquely fruitless. In fact, Defendants concede that Plaintiffs' seven terminated grants are 'comparable' to awards to grantees in Red States that were not terminated."

That decision vacated the termination of seven DOE grants. Last month in American Institute of Chemical Engineers v. Wright, Mehta approved a stipulated judgment that restored 11 more DOE grants.

In both of those cases, the government conceded that "a primary reason for the selection of which DOE grant termination decisions were included in the October 2025 notice tranche was whether the grantee was located in a 'Blue State.'" The government also agreed that "it would be legally sufficient for equal protection purposes to find that a primary reason for the termination decisions at issue is because of location in blue states."

Leaving aside the equal protection issue, the use of grant cancellations to penalize the president's political opponents is part of a broader pattern. Trump has not hesitated to use the levers of federal power in service of his personal interests, whether to enrich himself or to inflict pain on his foes. He has used regulatory threats to chill constitutionally protected speech, perverted the criminal justice system to punish critics for saying things he did not like, and issued executive orders that posed an existential threat to law firms that had represented clients or causes he abhors. Rescinding grants for partisan reasons is business as usual for a president who routinely weaponizes the government against his enemies.
